Internet & networking · 8/8

0-RTT early data and replay

1-RTT data

  • Sent after the handshake
  • Forward secret
  • Server Random blocks replay

0-RTT early data

  • Sent in the first flight with a PSK
  • No forward secrecy guarantee
  • Can be replayed between connections

Send early data only when a replay does no harm.

Before the first HTTPS request,

the browser and the server must agree on secret keys.

TLS 1.3 does this in one round trip.

The browser sends ClientHello.

It carries a key share, the server name,

called SNI, and the protocols it speaks, called ALPN.

The server answers with ServerHello and its own key share.

Now both sides compute the same handshake keys.

Neither side sends the keys.

Everything after ServerHello is encrypted.

The server sends EncryptedExtensions, which carries the chosen ALPN protocol,

then Certificate, CertificateVerify and Finished.

Certificate names the server.

Anyone can copy a certificate,

so CertificateVerify signs the transcript with the private key.

Finished proves that nobody changed the handshake.

The browser checks the signature and the MAC,

then sends its own Finished.

Its first HTTP request follows at once as encrypted application data.

Count the trips.

One flight goes out, one flight comes back, then the request leaves.

That is one round trip.

A key share mismatch adds a second trip.

A returning browser can skip the wait.

With a pre-shared key from an earlier visit,

it sends early data in the first flight.

An attacker can replay that data, so send only safe requests.
